result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.graph_edit_distance()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute the approximate graph edit distance between this graph and another. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L21420-L21519){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.graph_edit_distance( other, node_cost=1.0, edge_cost=1.0, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Graph edit distance](/assets/graphs/graph-edit-distance.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Graph G has nodes A, B, C, D and H has A, B, D, E; both share edges A–B and B–D. Turning G into H deletes node C and edge A–C (accent in G) and inserts node E and edge D–E (accent in H): four edits at cost 1 each, so the distance is 4." width="100%"} Counts the minimum number of node insertions, node deletions, edge insertions, and edge deletions to transform this graph into the other. Uses label-based matching (exact label match = same node). Nodes are matched by label (an unlabelled node is represented by its ID as a string), and edges by the labels of their endpoints. A node whose label exists only in `other=` costs one node insertion and a node whose label exists only in the calling graph costs one node deletion; edges are counted the same way. Each count is multiplied by its cost and the products are summed into `distance`. Because the node correspondence is fixed by the labels, there is no search over possible node mappings: the method runs in linear time and is "approximate" only in the sense that it does not look for a cheaper relabelling. Two structurally identical graphs with different labels therefore get a large distance. This is useful for: - quantifying how far a network has moved between two snapshots or conditions - scoring a reconstructed network against a reference network on the same entities - ranking several candidate networks by how close they are to a target Edges follow the same rules as `edge_overlap()`: in undirected graphs `A--B` equals `B--A`, weights and attributes are ignored, and parallel edges count once. Edges attached to a deleted or inserted node are counted as separate edge edits as well. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [other]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The target graph. The distance measures the cost of turning the calling graph into this one. It should normally have the same directedness as the calling graph. With the default unit costs the distance is symmetric, so swapping the graphs only swaps the insertion and deletion counts. [node_cost]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1.0]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Cost charged for each node insertion or deletion. The default is `1.0`. Set it to `0.0` to count only edge changes, or raise it to make changes to the node set weigh more than rewiring. [edge_cost]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1.0]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Cost charged for each edge insertion or deletion. The default is `1.0`. Like `node_cost=`, this only scales the `distance` value; the individual counts in the result are unaffected. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Dictionary with float values under these keys: - `distance`: the total cost, `(node_insertions + node_deletions) * node_cost + (edge_insertions + edge_deletions) * edge_cost`. - `node_insertions`, `node_deletions`: the number of node labels found only in `other=` and only in the calling graph, respectively. - `edge_insertions`, `edge_deletions`: the number of edges found only in `other=` and only in the calling graph, respectively. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~edge_overlap`) : Compare edge sets with a Jaccard index. [](`~differential_edges`) : List which edges were added or removed. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Turning `g` into `h` requires deleting node `C` and its edge `A--C`, then inserting node `E` and the edge `D--E`. That is one edit of each kind, for a total distance of `4.0`: ::: {#733407f2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "D"), ("A", "C")]) ) h = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "D", "E"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "D"), ("D", "E")]) ) g.graph_edit_distance(h) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'node_deletions': 1.0, 'distance': 4.0, 'edge_insertions': 1.0, 'edge_deletions': 1.0, 'node_insertions': 1.0} ``` ::: ::: The costs only change how the counts are weighted. With `node_cost=0.0` the two node edits are free, so only the two edge edits remain: ::: {#d5c39fc0 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} g.graph_edit_distance(h, node_cost=0.0)["distance"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 2.0 ``` ::: :::
